Chatbots: 51% of customers dislike being kept from a real person

Chatbots have become a fixture of customer service. They answer day and night, handle simple questions and take pressure off teams. But on the customer side, the reception is more mixed, and has been for a long time.

Back in 2018, according to Statista's dossier on customer service in the US, just under 51% of Americans surveyed said they disliked chatbots because they keep them from reaching a live person. More recent data shows that customers use these tools, but still prefer a human conversation when they can have one.

What customers hold against chatbots

The main complaint is not the quality of answers but the feeling of being blocked. A customer with an unusual or urgent problem wants to talk to someone who can understand their situation. A chatbot that goes in circles or points to an FAQ creates frustration.

That 2018 figure is still instructive today, even though chatbots have improved a lot since. It is a reminder that automation is seen as an obstacle as soon as it prevents access to a human.

The more important or emotional the issue, the stronger this need. Nobody wants to explain a billing error or a damaged delivery to a script that does not understand them.

Chat, yes, but with a person

In 2022, according to the same dossier, 61% of Americans considered chatting with an agent the easiest customer service channel to use. Only 23% chose live video chat.

So the conversational format works. What makes the difference is having a person who can understand and act. Customers like the speed and simplicity of chat, but they expect a real answer to their problem.

Chat combines the advantages of writing, such as keeping a record, with those of a human conversation. Companies that fully replace the agent with a bot lose precisely what made the channel popular.

Usage is growing anyway

Chatbots are not rejected outright. According to Statista's dossier on AI and extended reality in e-commerce, in 2024, almost half of customers used chatbots to schedule appointments, around 47% to help place orders and 46% to report an issue or start a return.

For simple, well-defined tasks, they are helpful. And trust is slowly improving: in 2025, 32% of US furniture shoppers believed a chatbot provided the same quality of information as a sales associate, according to the dossier on AI in US e-commerce.

In other words, two thirds of them still thought otherwise.

Every conversation is data about the customer

A chatbot does not end the conversation with the customer. It records part of it. Each exchange holds valuable information: the question asked, the words used, the moment the customer gives up, the request to speak to a person, the irritation expressed.

These conversations are rarely analyzed. Companies measure the chatbot's resolution rate but pay little attention to what customers write in it. They miss the clearest signals: the topics the chatbot cannot handle, and the customers who leave unhappy.

We covered this point in our article on AI in e-commerce customer service.

Analyzing chatbot conversations

Automatic language analysis can read every chatbot conversation, just like emails, tickets and calls. It spots unresolved requests, recurring phrasing, emotions expressed and the moments when customers ask to speak to someone.

That information helps improve the chatbot itself, route customers to a human more smoothly when needed, and fix the causes of contacts. The models used are Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case, and data stays hosted in France.

For contact centers, our call centers page describes this multichannel approach.

Finding the right balance

The right model is neither fully automated nor fully human. It is a chatbot that handles simple requests quickly, hands over without friction, and whose conversations are analyzed so it keeps improving. Customers accept automation when it helps them; they reject it when it holds them back.

In practice, it helps to track three indicators each month: the share of conversations where the customer asks for a human, the topics where the chatbot fails most often, and the tone of messages at the end of the exchange. These three numbers say more than the resolution rate about whether the chatbot really helps.

They also show where to invest next: better answers, smoother handovers or fixing the underlying problem.

What this means for you

Your customers use chatbots, but want to be able to reach a person. custovox.ai analyzes your chatbot conversations, along with your emails and calls, to spot unresolved requests and the moments when frustration rises.
